title: Anti-AI-patterns guide: the tells that make AI-written content obvious — and how to strip them

sections.title: Why a strip-list beats a smarter prompt
sections.html:
When you tell a model to "sound less like AI," it doesn't know what you mean, so it keeps every tell and adds adjectives to compensate. You get a longer draft carrying the same signals.

The fix is mechanical. A model is very good at find-and-replace against a named pattern. It is very bad at the vague vibe of "be more human." Name the 14 patterns, give it the rewrite rule for each, and the quality jump shows up immediately.

The model never failed to write like you. Nobody handed it the list of tells to cut for this exact job. Once you do, the job becomes search-and-strip, which models do near-perfectly.

One client's posts were dying at zero reach because they read like a corporate newsletter. Same voice inputs, same model. We added the strip-list, the posts started passing as his own writing, and he now spends about 10 minutes a week approving them.

sections.title: The 14 tells (and the exact strip for each)
sections.html:
Each row: the pattern, how to catch it, and the before → after so you can watch the fix land.

#The tellHow to find itBefore → After
1Corrective-contrast flipRegex: (isn'taren'tnot justnot only).{0,20}(it'?sthey'?re)Before: a clause that denies the plain reading, then swaps in a loftier one, welded into one breath. After: state the loftier claim once, then back it with a number. *(Shown as description on purpose: the literal pattern fails the very scan we are building.)*
2Era-setting openerSearch drafts' first sentence for "world / landscape / age / pace / evolving""As the business world keeps accelerating, companies must adapt." → "Three of my clients lost a full day a week to manual reporting."
3Inflated value verbsWord list: utilize, facilitate, spearhead, harness, supercharge, streamline, optimize, empower"We utilize AI to facilitate growth." → "We use AI to cut your reporting time."
4Rule-of-three triadsFlag any "X, Y, and Z" list of abstract nouns"faster, smarter, and more efficient" → "you save 6 hours a week."
5Dramatic em-dash pauseCount em-dashes; flag more than one per 300 words"The result, well, it changed everything." → "The result changed how he books work."
6Adjective stackingFlag two+ adjectives before a noun"a powerful, intuitive, game-changing tool" → "a tool that drafts your posts."
7Hedge throat-clearString match: "it's worth noting", "needless to say", "as we all know""It's worth noting that consistency matters." → "Post 3 times a week or the algorithm forgets you."
8Latinate connectorsWord list: additionally, consequently, thus, hence, therefore"Additionally, this drives results." → "It booked him two calls last month."
9Hollow wrap-up openerMatch: "to wrap up", "when all is said and done", "at the end of the day""When all is said and done, AI is here to stay." → (delete the sentence; end on the last concrete point.)
10Fake-intimacy pivotMatch: "here's the thing", "but here's the kicker", "let that sink in""Here's the thing: most people get this wrong." → "Most people skip the QA step. It costs them the reach."
11Audience catch-allRegex: whether you'?re.{0,40}or"Whether you're a founder or a freelancer, this helps." → "If you approve content for a client, this saves you the editing pass."
12Over-hedged claimFlag stacked qualifiers: can / may / might / often / generally"This can often potentially help improve results." → "This cut his editing time to 10 minutes a week."
13Symmetrical rhythmFlag 3+ consecutive sentences of near-equal lengthThree 14-word sentences in a row → break one to 4 words, run one long. Vary it like speech.
14Decorated bullets + overpromising headersFlag emoji bullets and Title-Case headers richer than their section"🚀 Game-Changing Strategies" over two thin lines → plain header that states what the section actually gives.

sections.title: Watch three fixes land
sections.html:
Picking the three that show up in almost every first draft.

  • Tell 3, inflated verbs: "We empower teams to harness AI and supercharge output." → "We set up the automations so your team stops copy-pasting between tools." The second one says what literally happens.
  • Tell 1, corrective-contrast: the model loves bolting a denial onto a grand claim in one sentence. Strip the denial, keep the claim, add the proof. The rhythm stops sounding like a TED slide.
  • Tell 5, em-dash pause: the model uses the dash as a drumroll. A human writing fast just starts a new sentence. Replace the dash with a period and you instantly read more like talking.
If a sentence sounds like a SaaS landing page, it is a tell. Swap it for what literally happened, with a number attached, and it reads like a person who did the work.

sections.title: Role
sections.html: You are a line editor. Your only job is to find and remove machine-written tells from a draft, then return the cleaned draft. Preserve the author's meaning, claims, numbers, and structure. Change wording only where a tell fires. Do not add new ideas. Do not lengthen the draft.

sections.title: Process
sections.html:
1. Read the draft once.
  2. Run every rule below in order.
  3. Rewrite each flagged span using the rule's fix.
  4. Return: (a) the cleaned draft, (b) a bullet list of what you changed,
one line per fix, format: "Tell N: -> ".

sections.title: The 14 rules
sections.html:
1. CORRECTIVE-CONTRAST FLIP
Find: a sentence that negates a plain reading and pivots to a grander claim in the same breath. Regex aid: (isn't|aren't|not just|not only) within ~20 chars of (it's|they're). Fix: delete the negation. State the grander claim once. Add a fact.
  1. ERA-SETTING OPENER
Find: an opening sentence about the times, the pace, the industry's evolution, or the modern world. Fix: replace with the sharpest concrete observation or number you have.
  1. INFLATED VALUE VERBS
Find: utilize, facilitate, spearhead, harness, supercharge, streamline, optimize, empower, and any verb that sounds like a software pitch. Fix: swap for the plain action verb (use, build, cut, fix, send, grow).
  1. RULE-OF-THREE TRIADS
Find: lists of three abstract adjectives or nouns ("faster, smarter, X"). Fix: keep one concrete item, or replace the triad with one result.
  1. DRAMATIC EM-DASH PAUSE
Find: more than one em-dash per ~300 words, or any em-dash used as a suspense beat. Fix: replace with a period and a new sentence.
  1. ADJECTIVE STACKING
Find: two or more adjectives stacked before a noun. Fix: keep at most one, or drop all and let the noun stand.
  1. HEDGE THROAT-CLEAR
Find: "it's worth noting", "needless to say", "as we all know", "make no mistake". Fix: delete the phrase. Keep the point that followed it.
  1. LATINATE CONNECTORS
Find: additionally, consequently, thus, hence, therefore, as a glue word at a sentence start. Fix: delete it, or replace with how a person actually links ideas (and, so, but), or start a fresh sentence.
  1. HOLLOW WRAP-UP OPENER
Find: "to wrap up", "when all is said and done", and similar closers. Fix: delete the whole sentence. End on the last concrete point.
  1. FAKE-INTIMACY PIVOT
Find: "here's the thing", "but here's the kicker", "let that sink in". Fix: delete the pivot. State the point directly.
  1. AUDIENCE CATCH-ALL
Find: "whether you're a X or a Y" framing. Fix: name the one reader who actually benefits and what they get.
  1. OVER-HEDGED CLAIM
Find: stacked qualifiers (can, may, might, often, generally) that drain the claim. Fix: cut the hedges. Make one direct assertion backed by a number.
  1. SYMMETRICAL RHYTHM
Find: three or more sentences in a row of near-equal length. Fix: break one to under 6 words. Let one run long. Vary it like speech.
  1. DECORATED BULLETS + OVERPROMISING HEADERS
Find: emoji bullets, and Title-Case headers richer than their section. Fix: plain bullets. Rewrite the header to state what the section gives.

sections.title: Hard rules
sections.html:
• Never invent facts, numbers, or claims to replace a stripped phrase.
If a fix needs a fact you do not have, mark it [ADD A NUMBER HERE].
  • Keep the author's voice and length. Strip, do not embellish.
  • Your own output must pass all 14 rules. Self-check before returning.

sections.title: How to run it on every draft
sections.html:
• Load it once: drop the skill into Claude as a project skill or paste it above any draft you want cleaned.
  • Run before any human reads: the strip pass is the first gate, so your editor only ever sees copy that has already lost its tells.
  • Time cost: the manual version of this is roughly 20 to 30 minutes a post of hunting and rewriting. The skill does it in one pass, and you spend the saved time on the one or two judgment calls that actually need you.
